title: Warning and alarm clarity improvement
summary: Creative Navy improves alarm and warning clarity by defining priority structures, redundant communication channels, actionable messages, mute behaviour, recovery indication, and warning architecture within specific product interfaces. The documented evidence spans IEC 60601-1-8 and IEC 62366-1 alarm work, redundant cue design for theatre conditions, multi-engine fault prioritisation, consumer alert tiering, silent failure warnings in simulation software, embedded vehicle warning redesign, and ISA-18.2 / IEC 62682 industrial alarm rationalisation.
keyFacts: Alert fatigue occurs when users encounter too many alarms or too many low-priority alarms, with false positives and nuisance alarms identified as primary drivers.
An actionable warning communicates both the problem and what to do about it; a warning without a next action is not actionable in time-pressured environments.
IEC 60601-1-8 requires alarm differentiation beyond colour for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment.
The Kardion MCS Controller alarm architecture was shaped by IEC 62366-1 usability-engineering hazards and IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements.

The Kardion design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required; Creative Navy's role was formative only, with summative validation and regulatory submission remaining the manufacturer's responsibility.
In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, critical states and warnings were communicated through spatial position, icon form, and colour rather than colour alone.
In the Cox Marine cluster displays case, a two-level alarm architecture combined a fault-summary area with per-tile alarm highlighting for multi-engine configurations.
In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, configuration errors fell from 5–8 to 1–2 and corrective load fell from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes.

In the Stromer e-bike embedded display case, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of issues requiring user intervention before redesign and did not appear on the issues list after redesign in repeated tests.
In the Gericke industrial HMI case, repeat alarms more than halved at three sites: 42% to 18%, 58% to 28%, and 73% to 35%, with results client-measured by Gericke.

bodySections.heading: Warning and alarm clarity improvement in product interfaces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Warning and alarm clarity improvement is the design capability concerned with making alarm states, warnings, alerts, recovery signals, mute states, and fault hierarchies understandable, distinguishable, actionable, and difficult to miss under the operating conditions of a specific product.

This capability is product-level design work. It addresses how alarm clarity is designed inside specific interfaces, including alarm layers, overlays, message content, visual hierarchy, cue redundancy, recovery indication, and the relationship between warnings and the rest of the screen.

bodySections.heading: When warning and alarm clarity is needed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Warning and alarm clarity is needed when a product can signal a condition that users must notice, interpret, prioritise, and act on. The design problem is not only whether an alarm appears. The design problem is whether the alarm directs attention to the right condition, communicates urgency, gives the user a next action when action is required, and remains visible enough that it cannot be forgotten.

Alert fatigue, also called alarm fatigue, occurs when users encounter too many alarms or too many low-priority alarms. False positives and nuisance alarms are identified in the documented evidence as primary drivers of alert fatigue. In process-industry settings, repeat-alarm rate is used as a measure of nuisance-alarm burden.

Actionability is separate from visibility. An actionable warning communicates both what is wrong and what to do. In time-pressured environments, a warning that communicates a problem without a next action is not actionable.

bodySections.heading: What Creative Navy defines in warning and alarm clarity work
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's warning and alarm clarity work defines the structural rules that govern how warnings, overlays, alarm layers, and interruptive elements relate to the product interface. This structural logic is warning architecture, and it must be established before individual warning components are designed.

The capability includes priority tiering, where alarm states are ranked by urgency and made visually distinguishable. It includes visual differentiation beyond colour, because colour alone can become unreliable under variable lighting, divided attention, night-vision constraints, gloves, vibration, or other operating conditions.

The capability also includes mute behaviour and recovery indication. A muted alarm must remain visually present at reduced prominence and must not be dismissible into a state where an active alarm is invisible. A recovery indication tells users that a previously alarmed condition has resolved, so they can confirm whether their action was effective.

In expert software, warning and alarm clarity can also include silent failure warnings. Silent failure occurs when a process completes normally while producing output that appears valid but is structurally incorrect. In that context, warnings must interrupt the failure before or after the system produces misleading output.

bodySections.heading: Regulated alarm architecture in the Kardion MCS Controller
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Kardion MCS Controller case is the most formal documented alarm-architecture example. The alarm architecture was derived from use-related hazards identified through the IEC 62366-1 usability-engineering process, while the alarm-system requirements were set by IEC 60601-1-8 for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment.

Creative Navy's design work for Kardion included priority tiering, visual differentiation beyond colour, mute behaviour, and explicit alarm state visibility. The absence of an alarm had to be confirmable as a system state; operators needed to confirm that no active alarms existed, rather than merely observe the absence of an alarm indicator.

The Kardion alarm requirements constrained the standard view by reserving some spatial positions and visual treatments for the alarm layer. That removed those options from the nominal state hierarchy and clarified the remaining option space for the interface.

The regulatory result is recorded as FDA approval: the design passed evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required. The alarm architecture contributed to the review satisfying identified use-related hazards related to alarm misinterpretation and missed alarms. Creative Navy's role was formative only; summative validation and regulatory submission were the manufacturer's responsibility.

bodySections.heading: Redundant warning cues in the deSoutter Medical / Zethon device
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The deSoutter Medical / Zethon case shows alarm-channel design under variable operating conditions. Benchmarking found that most of the 6 comparable devices used colour as the primary, and often sole, indicator of device state and warning conditions. Under variable theatre lighting, including repositioned surgical headlights and adjusted overhead illumination, colour coding becomes unreliable.

Creative Navy's design response used three independent communication channels for every critical state and warning: spatial position, icon form, and colour. Spatial position made the indicator readable when colour and icon form were unclear. Icon form carried meaning independently of colour. Colour remained present but was no longer the only cue.

The design decision was governed by IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation and directly addressed the use-related hazard of state misinterpretation under operating theatre conditions. Surgeon feedback from design review sessions reported that state verification was reduced to brief glance recognition. That statement is design review session feedback, not post-deployment measurement.

bodySections.heading: Fault prioritisation in Cox Marine cluster displays
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Cox Marine cluster displays case addresses a fault-prioritisation problem in multi-engine configurations. When several engines are present, an alarm must direct attention to the priority engine, not merely signal that a fault exists somewhere.

Creative Navy identified the issue during scenario testing in Concept Convergence. Designs that passed nominal-state evaluation failed the multi-engine fault scenario because they surfaced fault presence without directing attention. A design that requires captains to scan 6 tiles for a fault source under time pressure is treated as a design failure even if the fault indicator is technically visible.

The resulting two-level alarm architecture used a dedicated fault-summary area to surface the highest-priority condition across all engine tiles, followed by per-tile alarm highlighting so captains could confirm the source. A military night vision mode added a hard constraint: all alarm states, including the two-level structure, had to remain distinguishable under night vision goggles.

bodySections.heading: Alert tiering for a non-technical consumer audience
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Elsner Elektronik case shows why alarm wording and priority must match the user's ability to act. The consumer embedded-device audience included non-technical occupants who could not address sensor faults directly. A technical fault code presented to someone who cannot interpret it is not an effective alarm; it becomes noise that trains users to ignore later alarms.

Creative Navy's design response used a dual-priority alert system. General alerts covered routine conditions such as a sensor outside the preferred range, calibration drift, or delayed readings. They used low-urgency visual and auditory signalling and communicated that something could be adjusted or that an engineer should be informed when convenient.

Critical notifications covered complete sensor failure and safety-relevant state changes. They used distinct visual treatment and escalated auditory signalling to communicate that something required immediate attention. The distinction was calibrated to the audience: general alert meant something to know about; critical notification meant something to act on now.

bodySections.heading: Silent failure warnings in Gexcon CFD simulation software
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Gexcon CFD simulation case addresses silent failure in expert software. The error did not stop the system. The simulation could complete normally and produce output that appeared valid, while the configuration was structurally incorrect.

Before redesign, available case evidence records 5–8 configuration errors per simulation, each requiring 4–6 hours of corrective work. The warning architecture addressed the problem at three points in the workflow: during scenario setup, at contradictory inputs, and at post-run error detection.

During scenario setup, warnings surfaced incomplete required values before the simulation ran. At contradictory inputs, warnings surfaced internally contradictory values before the simulation was initiated. At post-run error detection, warnings specified the error, its location in the configuration, and the corrective action.

Each warning was designed against an actionability standard: the user had to understand both what was wrong and what to do. The documented outcome was a reduction in configuration errors from 5–8 to 1–2, and a reduction in corrective load from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes.

bodySections.heading: Warning architecture in the Stromer e-bike embedded display
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Stromer e-bike embedded display case shows why warning architecture must be defined before warning components. A previous external agency had designed the screen architecture first and then added warnings as overlays. The warnings had no native relationship to the surface they were placed on.

The consequences were observable and classifiable. Warnings covered screen content they should not cover. Warnings interfered with active interactions. Some warnings were too persistent, while others were too easily dismissed. Some warnings appeared without enough context for riders to understand what they referred to.

The product carried safety warnings, status alerts, error states, and threshold notifications. EN 15194:2017 specified requirements for warning device symbology and behaviour. Regulatory colour conventions constrained some decisions, including a tyre pressure sensor workstream where yellow was specified for sensor malfunction states while severity logic called for red.

Creative Navy redesigned the layout and overlay system, the information architecture, and the rules governing how warnings and interruptive elements relate to the screen structure. Before the redesign, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of all issues rated as requiring user intervention. After the redesign, warnings did not appear on the issues list in repeated tests.

bodySections.heading: Industrial alarm rationalisation in the Gericke HMI
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Gericke industrial HMI case is the documented industrial alarm-management example. The relevant alarm-management frameworks were ISA-18.2 and IEC 62682. Gericke operated in GMP environments, with GAMP 5 relevant; it was not a regulated device and was not governed by IEC 62366-1.

The legacy interface showed two central failure modes together. It had no priority hierarchy: operator testing found operators attending to the most visible alarm rather than the most relevant alarm. It also produced alarm flooding, where a single fault generated a cascade of secondary alarms handled symptom by symptom. Alarms were raw error codes with no corrective path, requiring manual lookup.

Creative Navy's design response combined alarm rationalisation with a root-cause hierarchy. Secondary alarms were collapsed beneath their originating event, and probable cause was indicated so operators could address the cause rather than chase effects. Contextual alarm explanations replaced raw codes with plain explanations of the condition and what to do.

The measured alarm-quality outcome was repeat-alarm rate, the process-industry measure of nuisance-alarm burden. Results were client-measured by Gericke at three sites within a confirmed single-variable window: 42% to 18% at a Swiss pharma site, 58% to 28% at an Italian food site, and 73% to 35% at a Swiss chemicals site. Fault-diagnosis time fell over the same period from 24 to 8 minutes, 38 to 12 minutes, and 68 to 20 minutes.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and limits of warning and alarm clarity improvement
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Warning and alarm clarity improvement is not the same as the full alarm-management discipline. Alarm management includes lifecycle, standards regimes, and process governance; this capability addresses how Creative Navy designs alarm clarity in specific product interfaces.

Regulated medical-device alarm work must keep formative design work separate from summative validation and regulatory submission. In the Kardion case, Creative Navy's role was formative only; summative validation and regulatory submission were the manufacturer's responsibility.

Not all evidence has the same strength. Stromer includes Creative Navy-designed and run field testing and Creative Navy-measured eye tracking. Gericke outcomes were client-measured by Gericke. DeSoutter surgeon feedback came from design review sessions. Gericke examples include reconstructions of the redesign rather than logged incidents.

Standards differ by context. IEC 60601-1-8 and IEC 62366-1 governed the Kardion alarm architecture. ISA-18.2 and IEC 62682 were relevant to Gericke's industrial alarm-management context. EN 15194:2017 constrained warning device symbology and behaviour in the Stromer e-bike workstream.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Warning and alarm clarity improvement addresses priority tiering, visual differentiation, mute behaviour, alarm state visibility, redundant cues, actionability, recovery indication, silent failure warnings, and warning architecture.

The Kardion MCS Controller alarm architecture was derived from IEC 62366-1 use-related hazards and IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements, and the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted with no design changes required.
In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, warning architecture reduced configuration errors from 5–8 to 1–2 and corrective load from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes.

In the Stromer e-bike embedded display case, Creative Navy-designed and run tests found that warnings accounted for approximately 30% of issues requiring user intervention before redesign and were absent from the issues list after redesign and again two years later.

In the Stromer e-bike embedded display case, eye tracking in actual riding conditions with 5 participants found average glance duration fell from 4.32 seconds to 1.89 seconds and glance frequency per kilometre fell by 18%.
weakerClaims: In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, critical states and warnings used spatial position, icon form, and colour because benchmarking found most of 6 comparable devices relied primarily or solely on colour.

In the Cox Marine cluster displays case, scenario testing found that nominal-state designs could fail the multi-engine fault scenario if they showed fault presence without directing attention to the priority engine.
In the Gericke industrial HMI case, repeat-alarm rates more than halved at three sites and fault-diagnosis time fell by roughly two-thirds over the same period.
limitations: The capability page distinguishes product-level warning and alarm clarity work from the broader alarm-management discipline.
The Kardion MCS Controller evidence is formative only; summative validation and regulatory submission are the manufacturer's responsibility.
The Kardion evidence records FDA approval but does not state an FDA pathway such as PMA or 510(k).
The deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgeon feedback is design review session feedback, not post-deployment measurement.
The Stromer evidence is Creative Navy-designed and run, including Creative Navy-measured eye tracking with 5 participants in actual riding conditions.
The Gericke industrial HMI outcomes were client-measured by Gericke, not Creative Navy-measured.
The Gericke conveying-blockage and refill-cycle examples are Creative Navy reconstructions of the redesign, not logged incidents.
Gericke is not a regulated device; it operates in GMP environments, with GAMP 5 relevant, and ISA-18.2 / IEC 62682 are the relevant alarm-management frameworks.
